title: Sequences and Series
tagline: Sequences and series, arithmetic and geometric progressions, arithmetic and geometric means, infinite geometric series, and standard special sums.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Mathematics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Mathematics registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers, and a series is the sum of the terms of a sequence. This chapter deals with two especially important kinds of sequences: arithmetic progressions, where each term increases by a fixed amount, and geometric progressions, where each term is multiplied by a fixed number. We study the general term and the sum of terms for both, the relations between arithmetic and geometric means, the special case of an infinite geometric series, and a few standard sums that appear again and again.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Arithmetic progression; arithmetic mean; geometric progression; finite and infinite geometric series; geometric mean; relation between A.M. and G.M.; standard special sums

learningOutcomes: Distinguish a sequence from a series.
Use the general term and sum formulas for A.P. and G.P.
Use the infinite G.P. sum when appropriate.
Use standard sum formulas for n, n^2 and n^3.

blocks.text: A sequence is a list of numbers written in a definite order, such as 2, 5, 8, 11, ... A series is what you get when you add the terms of a sequence, such as 2 + 5 + 8 + 11 + ... The distinction matters because many questions ask for a term of the sequence and others ask for the sum of several terms. An arithmetic progression has a constant difference between consecutive terms, and a geometric progression has a constant ratio.

items: A sequence is an ordered list.
A series is the sum of terms.
A.P. has a constant common difference.
G.P. has a constant common ratio.

items.text: 3, 7, 11, 15 is an A.P. with common difference 4. 3, 6, 12, 24 is a G.P. with common ratio 2.
items.note: The first is about addition of a fixed amount; the second is about repeated multiplication.

blocks.text: In an A.P. with first term a and common difference d, the nth term is T_n = a + (n-1)d, and the sum of the first n terms is S_n = n/2[2a + (n-1)d]. The formula for the nth term is useful when you want one specific term, and the sum formula is useful when you want the total of a block of terms. If three numbers are in A.P., the middle one is the arithmetic mean of the other two.

items: T_n = a + (n-1)d for an A.P.
Arithmetic mean of a and c is (a+c)/2.
The sum formula uses the number of terms n.

items.text: For the A.P. 3, 7, 11, 15, a = 3 and d = 4, so the 10th term is 3 + 9(4) = 39, and the sum of the first 10 terms is 10/2(3 + 39) = 210.
items.note: The same term 39 appears in both the nth term and the sum formula, which is a good check.

blocks.text: In a G.P. with first term a and common ratio r, the nth term is T_n = a r^{n-1}, and for r not equal to 1 the sum of the first n terms is S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r). If |r| is less than 1, the infinite geometric series has a finite sum S_infinity = a/(1 - r). The convergence condition is essential; if |r| is greater than or equal to 1, the infinite sum does not exist in the simple sense.

items: T_n = a r^{n-1} for a G.P.
S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r) for r not equal to 1.
S_infinity = a/(1 - r) when |r| < 1.
If |r| >= 1, the infinite sum is not finite.

items.text: For 3, 6, 12, 24, the 4th term is 3(2^3) = 24. The infinite sum does not exist here because r = 2, which is not less than 1.
items.note: The rule for an infinite sum is not just a formula; it has a condition that must be checked.

blocks.text: If a, A, c are in A.P., then A is the arithmetic mean of a and c, so A = (a+c)/2. If a, G, c are in G.P. and a and c are positive, then G is the geometric mean, so G = sqrt(ac). For positive numbers, the arithmetic mean is greater than or equal to the geometric mean. These ideas are useful for inserting numbers between two given numbers and for comparing averages.

items: Arithmetic mean = (a+c)/2.
Geometric mean = sqrt(ac) for positive numbers.
For positive numbers, A >= G.
Means are useful for inserting terms.

items.text: Between 2 and 8, the arithmetic mean is (2+8)/2 = 5, and the geometric mean is sqrt(2 x 8) = 4. Here 5 > 4, as expected.
items.note: The inequality A >= G is strict unless the two numbers are equal.

blocks.text: Several sums appear so often that it is worth knowing them directly. The sum of the first n natural numbers is n(n+1)/2. The sum of the squares of the first n natural numbers is n(n+1)(2n+1)/6. The sum of the cubes of the first n natural numbers is [n(n+1)/2]^2. These are used in many problems where terms are not given explicitly but follow a simple pattern.

items: Sum of first n natural numbers = n(n+1)/2.
Sum of squares = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.
Sum of cubes = [n(n+1)/2]^2.
These are standard results worth remembering.

items.text: The sum of the first 5 natural numbers is 5(6)/2 = 15, and the sum of the squares 1^2 + 2^2 + 3^2 + 4^2 + 5^2 is 5(6)(11)/6 = 55.
items.note: These formulas save time and reduce errors when summing long lists.

keyPoints: A sequence is an ordered list; a series is its sum.
A.P. has constant difference; G.P. has constant ratio.
A.P. nth term: a + (n-1)d; sum: n/2[2a + (n-1)d].
G.P. nth term: a r^{n-1}; sum: a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r).
Infinite G.P. sum = a/(1 - r) only if |r| < 1.
A.M. = (a+c)/2, G.M. = sqrt(ac) for positive a, c.
Standard sums for n, n^2 and n^3 are worth knowing.
examFocus: Before using the infinite G.P. sum, check that |r| < 1.
When finding the nth term of a G.P., remember the exponent is n-1, not n.

vocabulary.meaning: The sum of the terms of a sequence.
A sequence in which each term differs from the previous one by a constant amount.
A sequence in which each term is multiplied by a constant to get the next.
The fixed amount added in an arithmetic progression.
The fixed multiplier in a geometric progression.

questions.prompt: The nth term of an A.P. with first term a and common difference d is:
questions.commonMistake: Using n instead of n-1 in the formula.

questions.prompt: For a G.P. with r = 2, the infinite sum:
options: Does not exist as a finite sum
questions.answer: Does not exist as a finite sum
questions.explanation: An infinite G.P. sum exists only if |r| < 1.
questions.commonMistake: Applying a/(1 - r) without checking the value of r.

questions.prompt: Find the 10th term and the sum of the first 10 terms of the A.P. 3, 7, 11, 15.
questions.explanation: Use the A.P. formulas with a = 3, d = 4.
questions.commonMistake: Using n instead of n-1, or mixing the sum and nth-term formulas.

questions.prompt: Insert one arithmetic mean between 6 and 14.
questions.explanation: The mean is exactly in the middle of the two numbers.
questions.commonMistake: Using the geometric mean, or adding the numbers without dividing by 2.

questions.prompt: Find the sum of the first 20 natural numbers and the sum of their squares.
questions.commonMistake: Using the wrong formula, or forgetting the factor in the square-sum formula.
